stem: Transfer of information from molecule of DNA to mRNA is called ____ process.
solution: Transcription is the process in which the genetic information stored in one strand of the DNA molecule is copied into a molecule of messenger RNA (mRNA) with the help of the enzyme RNA polymerase. Translation is the next step, in which the information in the mRNA is used to join amino acids into a protein on the ribosome; translocation is the transport of prepared food in plants; mutation is a sudden change in the genetic material. Hence the correct answer is Transcription.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
stem: Body breaks up into several fragments and each fragment starts to live as a new individual. This is ____ type of reproduction.
solution: In fragmentation the body of the organism breaks up into two or more fragments and each fragment grows into a complete new individual, e.g. Spirogyra. In budding a small bud arises on the parent body and separates (Hydra, yeast); in regeneration a lost or damaged body part is grown back (Planaria, star fish); in binary fission the single parent cell divides into two daughter cells (Amoeba, Paramoecium). Hence the answer is Fragmentation.

stem: Incomplete combustion of fuels leads to formation of ____
solution: When a carbon-containing fuel burns in a sufficient supply of oxygen, complete combustion occurs and carbon dioxide \(\text{CO}_2\) is formed. When the oxygen supply is insufficient, the carbon is only partly oxidised and poisonous carbon monoxide \(\text{CO}\) is produced. Chlorofluorocarbons are man-made refrigerant gases (not combustion products) and hydrogen sulphide comes from decay of sulphur-containing matter. Hence incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
stem: The spindle fibres start appearing from ____ stage of karyokinesis.
solution: Karyokinesis (division of the nucleus) has four stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. In prophase the chromatin condenses into chromosomes, the centrioles move to the opposite poles of the cell and the spindle fibres begin to appear between them (the nuclear membrane and nucleolus also start disappearing). In metaphase the already-formed spindle fibres only attach to the centromeres and align the chromosomes at the equator, in anaphase they contract and pull the chromatids apart, and in telophase they disappear. Hence spindle fibres start appearing in Prophase.

stem: Salts which can be used as supplement of calcium and iron are obtained from ____
solution: Gluconic acid is produced commercially by the fungus Aspergillus niger. Its salts — calcium gluconate and ferrous (iron) gluconate — are used as dietary supplements of calcium and iron respectively, because gluconate salts are easily absorbed and are not irritating to the stomach. Carbonic acid is unstable, acetic acid is used as vinegar and citric acid is used as a preservative and flavouring agent. Hence the answer is Gluconic acid.

stem: Find odd one out: Drying, Salting, Cooking, Soaking with sugar.
solution:
Odd one out: Cooking.
Drying, salting and soaking with sugar are all methods of FOOD PRESERVATION. They work by removing water or by making the water unavailable to micro-organisms (osmosis), so that bacteria and fungi cannot grow and the food does not spoil. Cooking is a method of preparing food (it may kill microbes temporarily but does not preserve the food), so it does not belong to this group.

stem: Write the correct co-relation: Annelida : Earthworm :: Platyhelminthes : ____
solution:
Platyhelminthes : Planaria.
Just as earthworm is an example of the phylum Annelida (segmented worms), Planaria is an example of the phylum Platyhelminthes (flatworms). Tapeworm and liver fluke are other acceptable examples of Platyhelminthes.

stem: State whether True/False: Tobacco containing substances cannot cause cancer of mouth and lungs.
solution:
False.
Tobacco contains nicotine and many other carcinogenic (cancer-causing) chemicals such as tar. Chewing tobacco, gutkha and mishri cause cancer of the mouth, tongue and throat, while smoking cigarettes and bidis causes cancer of the lungs. Hence tobacco-containing substances DO cause cancer of the mouth and lungs, so the statement is false.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
stem: Write function of testes.
solution:
Functions of the testes:
1. The testes are the male gonads. The seminiferous tubules in the testes produce the male gametes, i.e. sperms, by the process of spermatogenesis.
2. The interstitial cells of the testes secrete the male sex hormone testosterone, which brings about the development of the male reproductive organs and of the secondary sexual characters (deep voice, beard and moustache, broad chest, body hair) at puberty.

stem: I am connecting link between Reptilia and mammals. What is my name?
solution:
Duck-billed platypus (Ornithorhynchus).
The duck-billed platypus is an egg-laying mammal (a monotreme). Like reptiles it lays eggs and has a cloaca, but like mammals it has hair on the body and mammary glands with which it feeds milk to its young ones. Hence it is regarded as a connecting link between class Reptilia and class Mammalia. (Echidna, the spiny ant-eater, is another such connecting link.)

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
stem: Give scientific reason: Indians should follow family planning for controlling the population.
solution: India is the second most populous country in the world and its population is still growing rapidly because the birth rate is much higher than the death rate. Natural resources such as land, water, food, fuel and forests are limited, so a rapidly rising population puts a heavy burden on them and causes shortage of food, drinking water, housing, schools, hospitals and jobs. It also leads to poverty, unemployment, slums, deforestation and pollution, and lowers the standard of living and health of the people. Family planning (small family norm, proper spacing between two children and use of contraceptive methods) keeps the birth rate under control, so the available resources are enough for everyone and the health of the mother and the child also improves. Hence Indians should follow family planning for controlling the population.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
stem: Give scientific reason: We feel exhausted after exercising.
solution: During vigorous exercise the muscles need a large amount of energy, so they respire very fast. The supply of oxygen through the blood becomes insufficient to meet this demand. Therefore the muscle cells start carrying out ANAEROBIC respiration, in which glucose is incompletely broken down into lactic acid with the release of only a small amount of energy (2 ATP as against 38 ATP in aerobic respiration). The lactic acid accumulates in the muscles and causes muscle cramps, pain and fatigue, and the energy obtained is much less. Hence we feel exhausted after exercising. (On taking rest, extra oxygen is supplied, the lactic acid is oxidised and the fatigue disappears.)

stem: Give scientific reason: Hydroelectric energy, solar energy and wind energy are called renewable energies.
solution: Renewable sources of energy are those which are naturally replenished again and again and are practically inexhaustible, i.e. they are not exhausted by use. Water in rivers and dams is continuously renewed by the water cycle (rainfall), sunlight is received from the Sun every day and will be available for billions of years, and wind blows continuously because of the uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun. None of these three gets used up or finished, and all of them are pollution-free and available in nature free of cost. Hence hydroelectric energy, solar energy and wind energy are called renewable energies (unlike coal, petroleum and natural gas, which are limited and non-renewable).

stem: Complete the following chart showing the 'Effect of Radioactive Pollution' by writing the appropriate effect in each of the four blank boxes.
solution:
Effects of Radioactive Pollution (any four for the four boxes):
1. Harmful radiations damage the cells and tissues of the body, causing radiation burns, skin diseases and loss of hair.
2. They cause mutations (changes) in the DNA/genes, so hereditary defects and deformities appear in the next generations.
3. They cause serious diseases such as cancer, especially blood cancer (leukaemia), and tumours.
4. They weaken the immune system, cause anaemia, sterility (infertility) and even death of humans and animals.
5. Soil, water and air get contaminated, so crops, plants and aquatic life are destroyed and the whole ecosystem is disturbed for a very long time.
figureNote: Flow chart with a shaded central box labelled 'Effect of Radioactive Polution' [sic] and four blank boxes radiating from it (above, left, right and below), p-00.

stem: Distinguish between Aves and Mammalia.
solution:
Aves vs Mammalia:

| Aves | Mammalia |
|---|---|
| Body is covered with feathers | Body is covered with hair or fur |
| Fore limbs are modified into wings for flying | Fore limbs are usually modified into legs (or flippers/wings) for walking, swimming, etc. |
| Beak is present; teeth are absent | Beak is absent; teeth of different types are present in the jaws |
| They are oviparous — they lay eggs | They are mostly viviparous — they give birth to young ones (except platypus and echidna) |
| Mammary glands are absent | Mammary glands are present, which secrete milk to feed the young ones |
| Bones are hollow (pneumatic) and light; air sacs are present | Bones are solid; air sacs are absent |
| External ear (pinna) is absent | External ear (pinna) is generally present |
| Examples: pigeon, sparrow, crow, peacock | Examples: human, cow, bat, whale, dog |

stem: By observing the given picture, write any two effects of this disaster.
solution:
The picture shows a railway accident (train derailment) — a man-made disaster. Any two of its effects:
1. Loss of human life — many passengers are killed and a large number of people are seriously injured or become permanently disabled.
2. Heavy loss of property — the coaches, the engine, the railway track and the goods being carried are damaged, causing a huge financial loss.
3. Rail traffic on that route is disrupted for a long time, so transport of passengers and goods is stopped and normal life is affected.
4. The families of the victims suffer mental shock, trauma and loss of their earning members, and rescue and relief work has to be undertaken urgently.
figureNote: Photograph of a derailed train — coaches and engine overturned and piled on a damaged railway track with people standing nearby, p-01.

stem: Explain four ways to minimize stress.
solution:
Four ways to minimise stress:
1. Regular exercise, yoga, pranayama and meditation: these relax the body and the mind, improve concentration and reduce anxiety.
2. Adequate sleep, rest and a balanced diet: sound sleep of 7–8 hours and nutritious food keep the body and mind fresh and able to face difficulties.
3. Proper planning and time management: dividing work into parts, preparing a time-table, setting realistic goals and avoiding last-minute pressure prevents stress from building up.
4. Sharing and recreation: talking freely about one's problems with parents, teachers or friends, taking help of a counsellor when necessary, and spending time on hobbies, music, sports, reading and social activities lightens the mind and relieves stress.

stem: Complete the following conceptual picture on the uses of 'Microbes' by writing the appropriate use in each of the four blank boxes. (Two boxes are already filled as 'Oil spill' and 'Biogas and Composting'.)
solution:
Uses of microbes (the four blank boxes can be filled with any four of the following):
1. Medicines — production of antibiotics such as penicillin and streptomycin, and of vaccines and enzymes.
2. Food industry — production of curd, cheese, yoghurt, bread, idli and dosa batter by Lactobacillus and yeast.
3. Fermentation industry — production of alcohol, vinegar (acetic acid), citric acid, gluconic acid and lactic acid.
4. Biofertilizers and nitrogen fixation — Rhizobium, Azotobacter and blue-green algae increase soil fertility.
5. Sewage / waste-water treatment — microbes decompose the organic matter in sewage and purify the water.
(The two boxes already given show that microbes are also used to clear oil spills and to produce biogas and compost.)
figureNote: Concept map with a shaded central box 'Microbes' and six boxes joined to it by arrows — 'Oil spill' (top centre) and 'Biogas and Composting' (bottom left) are printed, the other four boxes are blank and to be completed, p-01.

stem: Explain the importance of Anatomical evidences with examples.
solution:
Anatomical evidences are obtained by studying and comparing the internal structure of the organs of different organisms. They are important because they show whether different organisms have a common ancestor, and thus prove that evolution has taken place.

1. Homologous organs: These organs have the SAME basic structure and origin but perform DIFFERENT functions. For example, the fore limbs of a human (grasping), a bat (flying), a whale (swimming), a horse (running) and a bird (flying) all contain the same bones — humerus, radius-ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges. This similarity shows that all these animals have evolved from a common ancestor and later became adapted to different environments. This is called divergent evolution.

2. Analogous organs: These organs have DIFFERENT basic structure and origin but perform the SAME function. For example, the wings of a bird (made of bones and feathers) and the wings of an insect (folds of the body wall) are both used for flying; similarly the flippers of a whale and of a penguin. Such organs show that unrelated organisms living in similar environments develop similar adaptations. This is called convergent evolution.

3. Vestigial organs: These are the reduced, functionless remains of organs that were well developed and useful in the ancestors, e.g. the vermiform appendix, the nictitating membrane of the eye, ear muscles and the tail bone (coccyx) in human beings. Their presence proves that man has evolved from ancestors in which these organs were functional.

Thus anatomical evidences establish the relationship between different groups of animals and support the theory of organic evolution.

context: What will you do? Why?
stem: Child of your neighbor is addicted to tobacco chewing. What will you do? Why?
solution:
What I will do: I will talk to the child affectionately and without scolding, and explain to him the harmful effects of tobacco. I will tell him that tobacco contains nicotine, which causes addiction, and many cancer-causing chemicals which lead to mouth ulcers, discoloured teeth, foul breath, loss of appetite, and cancer of the mouth, tongue, throat and lungs. I will show him posters/films on the ill-effects of tobacco, will encourage him to spend his time in sports, hobbies and good company, and will inform his parents. If necessary, I will suggest that he be taken to a doctor or to a de-addiction (rehabilitation) centre for counselling and treatment, and will keep encouraging him till he gives up the habit.

Why: Because tobacco addiction destroys physical and mental health, spoils studies and character, wastes money and can be fatal. It is at a young age that the habit can be broken most easily, and helping him is my social responsibility as a good neighbour and a responsible citizen.

context: What will you do? Why?
stem: Your friend has developed the hobby of snapping selfies. What will you do? Why?
solution:
What I will do: I will explain to my friend that taking selfies occasionally is not wrong, but making it a craze is dangerous. I will tell him about the many deaths that occur every year because people take selfies at risky places — on railway tracks, on the edge of cliffs, forts and waterfalls, near the sea, in front of moving vehicles or while driving. I will ask him never to take a selfie at a dangerous spot or while travelling, and to reduce the time spent on the mobile and on social media. I will involve him in sports, reading, music and other hobbies, will keep his company myself, and if the habit does not reduce I will inform his parents and suggest counselling.

Why: Because excessive selfie-taking ('selfie mania') is a form of behavioural addiction. It distracts attention and invites fatal accidents, and it also wastes time, harms studies and eyesight, and creates anxiety and a false need for likes and comments on social media, thereby damaging both physical and mental health.

context: What will you do? Why?
stem: Your sister has become incommunicative. She prefers to remain alone. What will you do? Why?
solution:
What I will do: I will spend more time with my sister, talk to her lovingly and patiently, and try to find out the cause of her behaviour — it may be failure in an examination, a quarrel, fear, insult, harassment, ill-health or some other stress. I will listen to her without blaming or making fun of her, will assure her of full support, and will encourage her to take part in games, exercise, yoga, meditation, music and family functions so that her mind becomes fresh. I will also tell my parents about it, and if she still remains withdrawn and depressed we will take her to a doctor or a professional counsellor/psychologist for proper guidance and treatment.

Why: Because remaining silent and alone for a long time is a sign of stress or depression, i.e. of poor mental health. If it is neglected, it can lead to loss of appetite and sleep, physical illness and even self-harm. Timely communication, family support and counselling relieve stress and restore her social and mental health.

stem: Which precautions are necessary for proper decomposition of domestic waste?
solution:
Precautions necessary for proper decomposition (composting) of domestic waste:
1. Segregation of waste: the biodegradable (wet) waste — vegetable and fruit peels, left-over food, dry leaves — must be separated from the non-biodegradable (dry) waste. Plastic, glass, metal, rubber, thermocol, batteries and e-waste must never be put in the compost pit, because they do not decompose and obstruct the process.
2. The waste should be cut or shredded into small pieces so that it decomposes quickly, and it should be spread in thin layers instead of a single thick heap.
3. Proper moisture must be maintained — the waste should be neither too dry nor too wet. Excess water fills the air spaces and stops decomposition.
4. Proper aeration (supply of oxygen) must be ensured by turning/mixing the heap from time to time, since most decomposer micro-organisms are aerobic.
5. The compost pit should be at a suitable distance from the house, away from a source of drinking water, in a shady place, and it should be covered with a layer of soil or a lid to avoid foul smell, flies, mosquitoes and stray animals.
6. A culture of decomposer micro-organisms, cow dung slurry or earthworms (vermicomposting) may be added to speed up the decomposition.
7. Waste containing oil, chemicals, medicines, insecticides or diseased material should not be added, as these kill the useful micro-organisms.

context: Observe the diagram of the animal given in the paper (a cockroach, with the parts Head, Thorax, Abdomen, Wings and Legs labelled) and answer the following questions.
stem: To which phylum does the animal included in the diagram belong?
solution: The animal shown in the diagram is a cockroach. It has a body divided into head, thorax and abdomen, three pairs of jointed legs, two pairs of wings and jointed appendages. Hence it belongs to the phylum ARTHROPODA (class Insecta).
figureNote: Labelled photograph/diagram of a cockroach with leader lines to Head, Thorax, Abdomen, Wings and Legs, p-01.

context: Observe the diagram of the animal given in the paper (a cockroach, with the parts Head, Thorax, Abdomen, Wings and Legs labelled) and answer the following questions.
stem: What is the exoskeleton made up of?
solution: The body of the cockroach (and of all arthropods) is covered by a hard exoskeleton (cuticle) which is made up of CHITIN, a tough nitrogen-containing polysaccharide. The chitinous exoskeleton protects the body and prevents loss of water; because it cannot grow, the animal sheds it from time to time by the process of moulting (ecdysis).

context: Observe the diagram of the animal given in the paper (a cockroach, with the parts Head, Thorax, Abdomen, Wings and Legs labelled) and answer the following questions.
stem: What is the symmetry?
solution: The cockroach shows BILATERAL SYMMETRY. Its body can be divided into two exactly equal (mirror-image) halves — a right half and a left half — by only ONE median longitudinal plane.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Explain the following concepts in short.
stem: Explain in short the concept: Surrogacy.
solution: Surrogacy: Some women are able to produce healthy ova and their husbands produce healthy sperms, but the woman cannot bear a pregnancy — for example her uterus is defective, has been removed, or pregnancy is dangerous for her health. In such cases the ovum of the wife and the sperm of the husband are fused in the laboratory (in vitro fertilization) and the embryo so obtained is implanted in the uterus of ANOTHER healthy, willing woman. This woman carries the pregnancy to full term and delivers the baby, after which the child is handed over to the biological parents. Such a woman is called a surrogate mother and the technique is called surrogacy ('surrogate' means substitute). The child is genetically the child of the biological parents, not of the surrogate mother.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Explain the following concepts in short.
stem: Explain in short the concept: In Vitro Fertilization (IVF).
solution: In Vitro Fertilization (IVF): 'In vitro' means 'in glass', i.e. outside the body. In some couples fertilization does not take place naturally — for example the fallopian tubes of the woman are blocked or the sperm count of the man is low. In IVF, mature ova are collected from the ovary of the woman and sperms are collected from the man, and the two are allowed to fuse in a sterile glass dish (petri dish) in the laboratory under controlled conditions. The zygote formed is allowed to divide, and the resulting embryo (at about the 8-cell stage) is implanted in the uterus of the woman, where further development takes place normally and a baby is born after the full term. A baby born by this technique is popularly called a 'test tube baby'.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Explain the following concepts in short.
stem: Explain in short the concept: Sperm Bank.
solution: Sperm Bank: A sperm bank (also called a semen bank or cryobank) is a place where semen collected from healthy, medically examined male donors is preserved. The donors are tested to make sure they are free from hereditary disorders and infectious diseases such as AIDS and hepatitis. The semen is then stored at a very low temperature in liquid nitrogen (about \(-196^\circ\text{C}\)) so that the sperms remain alive and viable for a long period. Whenever required, this preserved semen is supplied for artificial insemination or for IVF, so that couples in which the husband produces no sperms or very few sperms can still have a child.

stem: Label the body organization of human in the given figure by writing the name of the organ indicated by each of the boxes.
solution:
The figure shows the organ level of body organisation in the human being. Going from the head downwards, the indicated organs are:
1. Brain — the organ of the nervous system, present in the head, which controls and co-ordinates all the activities of the body.
2. Lungs — the pair of respiratory organs in the chest, in which exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide takes place.
3. Heart — the muscular pumping organ of the circulatory system, situated between the lungs.
4. Liver — the largest gland of the body, in the upper right part of the abdomen, which secretes bile.
5. Stomach — the bag-like organ of the digestive system in which food is churned and digested.
6. Muscles — the muscular tissue/organs of the limbs (e.g. of the thigh), which bring about movement of the body.

Thus a group of similar cells forms a tissue, different tissues together form an organ (brain, lungs, heart, liver, stomach), organs form an organ system, and all the organ systems together form the complete organism.

(Note: the exact organ against each box must be confirmed from the cropped figure.)
figureNote: Outline diagram of a human body showing internal organs (brain/head, lungs, heart, liver, stomach and thigh muscles) with six blank rectangular label-boxes joined to them by leader lines, p-02. Crop needed to confirm exactly which organ each box points to.

stem:
Complete the paragraph using proper words:

Spilling of petroleum oil occurs in ocean due to various reasons. This oil may prove fatal and toxic to ____ organisms. It is not easy to remove the oil layer from surface of water by ____ method. However, bacteria like ____ spp. and Alcanivorax borkumensis have the ability to destroy the pyridines and other chemicals. Hence, these ____ are used to clear the oil spills. solution:
Completed paragraph:

Spilling of petroleum oil occurs in ocean due to various reasons. This oil may prove fatal and toxic to AQUATIC organisms. It is not easy to remove the oil layer from surface of water by MECHANICAL method. However, bacteria like PSEUDOMONAS spp. and Alcanivorax borkumensis have the ability to destroy the pyridines and other chemicals. Hence, these BACTERIA are used to clear the oil spills. context: Attempts at various levels are performed for conserving environment. Which role would you like to perform? Give two actions each.
stem: Give two actions you would perform in the role of Prevention for conserving the environment.
solution:
Role — Prevention (stopping the damage before it occurs). Two actions:
1. Refuse and stop the use of plastic carry-bags, thermocol and other single-use plastic articles, and prevent the throwing of garbage, sewage and industrial effluents into rivers, lakes and the sea.
2. Prevent the cutting of trees (deforestation) and the hunting/poaching of wild animals, and prevent the unnecessary use of vehicles, loudspeakers, firecrackers and electricity so that air, noise and energy losses are avoided in the first place.

context: Attempts at various levels are performed for conserving environment. Which role would you like to perform? Give two actions each.
stem: Give two actions you would perform in the role of Control for conserving the environment.
solution:
Role — Control (keeping the existing pollution within safe limits). Two actions:
1. Control air pollution by getting vehicles serviced regularly and taking the PUC (pollution under control) certificate, by using public transport, bicycles or car-pooling, and by insisting that factories fit chimneys with filters, scrubbers and electrostatic precipitators.
2. Control water and land pollution by insisting on effluent treatment plants for industries and sewage treatment plants for towns, by segregating wet and dry waste at home, and by controlling the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides in farming.

context: Attempts at various levels are performed for conserving environment. Which role would you like to perform? Give two actions each.
stem: Give two actions you would perform in the role of Production for conserving the environment.
solution:
Role — Production (producing eco-friendly goods and energy). Two actions:
1. Produce and use energy from renewable, non-polluting sources — install solar panels, solar water heaters, solar cookers, biogas plants and wind mills instead of using coal-based electricity and LPG.
2. Produce eco-friendly materials — make compost and vermicompost from kitchen waste for use as organic manure, and produce paper bags, cloth bags and biodegradable/recycled articles in place of plastic ones.

context: Attempts at various levels are performed for conserving environment. Which role would you like to perform? Give two actions each.
stem: Give two actions you would perform in the role of Awareness for conserving the environment.
solution:
Role — Awareness (educating people). Two actions:
1. Organise rallies, street plays, poster and essay competitions, exhibitions and lectures in the school and the locality, and celebrate days such as World Environment Day, Earth Day, Van Mahotsav and Wildlife Week.
2. Spread the message of 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle', of tree plantation and of water conservation among neighbours, relatives and friends through pamphlets, wall-writings, social media, films and documentaries.

context: Attempts at various levels are performed for conserving environment. Which role would you like to perform? Give two actions each.
stem: Give two actions you would perform in the role of Conservation for conserving the environment.
solution:
Role — Conservation (protecting and preserving natural resources). Two actions:
1. Conserve water and soil — practise rain water harvesting, repair leaking taps, reuse water, build bunds and check dams, and stop soil erosion by planting trees and grass.
2. Conserve forests and wildlife — plant and look after trees (afforestation), protect sanctuaries, national parks and biosphere reserves, avoid articles made from animal skin, ivory and fur, and conserve energy by switching off unnecessary lights, fans and appliances.

context: Answer the following questions on biotechnology.
stem: What is Biotechnology?
solution: Biotechnology is the branch of science in which living organisms (micro-organisms, plant cells, animal cells) or their parts, cells, tissues and enzymes are used along with technological methods and engineering techniques to produce useful products or services for the welfare of human beings. It includes techniques such as tissue culture, genetic engineering (recombinant DNA technology), fermentation, cloning and stem-cell technology, and is applied in medicine, agriculture, industry and environmental management.

context: Answer the following questions on biotechnology.
stem: Give one use of Biotechnology.
solution: One use of biotechnology: it is used in medicine to produce life-saving medicines — for example, human insulin for the treatment of diabetes is produced by inserting the human insulin gene into the bacterium Escherichia coli. (Other uses: production of vaccines, antibiotics and interferon; gene therapy; production of disease-resistant and high-yielding crop varieties; tissue culture for rapid multiplication of plants; and treatment of sewage and oil spills.)

context: Answer the following questions on biotechnology.
stem: Give one commercial use of Biotechnology.
solution: One commercial use of biotechnology: the large-scale commercial production of genetically engineered human insulin (and of vaccines, antibiotics and enzymes) by pharmaceutical companies, which is sold all over the world. (Other commercial uses: commercial production of tissue-cultured saplings of banana, orchids, sugarcane and ornamental plants in nurseries; commercial cultivation of genetically modified crops such as Bt cotton; and industrial production of alcohol, vinegar, citric acid, cheese and bread by fermentation.)

context: Answer the following questions on biotechnology.
stem: Write two bacterial examples of biofertilizer.
solution: Two bacterial biofertilizers: (1) Rhizobium — it lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants and fixes atmospheric nitrogen, and (2) Azotobacter — a free-living soil bacterium that fixes atmospheric nitrogen. (Azospirillum and the phosphate-solubilising Bacillus are other bacterial biofertilizers; Nostoc and Anabaena are cyanobacterial biofertilizers used in paddy fields.)

context: Answer the following questions on biotechnology.
stem: Write two names of crops genetically developed.
solution: Two genetically developed (genetically modified) crops: (1) Bt cotton — the gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis has been inserted into cotton to make it resistant to the bollworm pest, and (2) Bt brinjal — similarly made pest-resistant. (Golden rice, which is enriched with beta-carotene (vitamin A), and genetically modified soybean, maize and tomato are other examples.)
